facts: Hydrochloric acid and some solutions containing halide ions attack the passive film on stainless steel.
Such attack "produce[s] corrosion of the pitting type."
Additions of molybdenum reduce the susceptibility to pitting corrosion.
payload.query: What corrosion mechanism does NBS Circular 592 associate with hydrochloric acid and other halide-containing solutions attacking stainless steel?
payload.answer:
Evidence-grounded answer:

- Hydrochloric acid and some solutions containing halide ions attack the passive film on stainless steel. [nbscircular592.pdf, p. 60, chunk 2b809bc1]
- Such attack "produce[s] corrosion of the pitting type." [nbscircular592.pdf, p. 60, chunk 2b809bc1]
- Additions of molybdenum reduce the susceptibility to pitting corrosion. [nbscircular592.pdf, p. 60, chunk 2b809bc1]

4.5. Hastelloy Alloys

The first of the high-nickel corrosion-resistant alloys known as Hastelloys were nickel-molyb¬ denum-iron alloys, but in subsequent alloys the composition was considerably changed. This dis¬ cussion will be confined to the corrosion-resistant alloys A, B, C, D, and F. Hastelloy R and Hastelloy X were designed for high-temperature mechanical properties, i. e., for super alloy service. Hastelloy A contains 56 Ni-22 Mo-22 Fe. It is usefully resistant to all concentrations of hydro¬ chloric acid at room temperature and to unaerated solutions at temperatures below about 160° F. It is usefully resistant to sulfuric acid of all concen¬ trations at temperatures up to about 160° F, and up to the boiling point for concentrations below 50 percent. open_questions: Circular 592 (in the provided evidence) does not give detailed mechanistic steps (electrochemical sequence) by which halide ions break down the passive film on stainless steel.

Circular 592 (in the provided evidence) does not specify concentration, temperature, or exposure-duration thresholds for onset of pitting by hydrochloric acid or halide-containing solutions on stainless steels.
